newsitem.title: UK: UK PSBR to hit target despite June data - analysts.
newsitem.headline: UK PSBR to hit target despite June data - analysts.

text.p: Britain's June public sector borrowing requirement may have come in above market expectations, but special factors were to blame, and the full year deficit will meet the government target, analysts said on Wednesday.
June's PSBR totalled 4.754 billion sterling, compared with a market consensus which saw the figure at 4.0 billion stg.

Analysts cited a change in the timing of VAT receipts and the new alignment of UK gilt interest payments for the higher-than-expected deficit, but said they expected July's PSBR to show a bounce-back.
"The PSBR reflects that people haven't taken adequately on board the change in VAT payments announced in the 1996 budget," said David Philpotts, UK economist at Schroders in London.

UK Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown earlier this month forecast the government's 1997/98 fiscal year PSBR, excluding windfall tax payments from Britain's privatised utilities, would hit 13.25 billion sterling.
This compares with a 23.1 billion pound deficit in 1996/97. If the windfall tax returns are included, the full-year PSBR is expected to total 10.9 billion stg.
"The (June) PSBR was always going to show a large deficit," said Darshini David, UK economist at HSBC.
"We were looking for 4.8 billion for June. The PSBR could continue to overshoot in the coming months, but I expect it to meet the government target for the full year."
Most gilt coupons payments have been realigned so interest payments are now made mainly in June and December, whereas previously payments were spread out across the year.
As a result, gilt coupon interest payments totalled 2.7 billion sterling in June according to the Office for National Statistics (ONS), compared with just 1.5 billion stg in June last year.
"The ONS reckon these factors (VAT and gilt payments) boosted last month's deficit by two billion pounds," said David Coleman, chief economist at CIBC Wood Gundy.
"We see no reason to disbelieve this explanation or for it to cast doubt on the Budget's PSBR forecast."
The PSBR figure could worry the gilt market in the short-term, but the full-year figure should be good news for gilts, David said.

Gilts were unshaken by the June PSBR, and by 1030 GMT were some 8/32 higher at 114-12, helped by a benign set of earnings data. UK average earnings for May showed a rise of 4.25 percent, down from April's figure of 4.5 percent.
Short sterling was higher across the board, with September short stg up 0.02 basis points at 92.85, and the December contract up 0.04 at 92.64.
